notes.b: The syllabus sets a minimum number of skills you must show in each group, so you can plan your performance around them. Agilities means the gymnastic skills performed on the floor, such as rolls, balances and cartwheels.
points: At least 2 jumps, 2 rolls, 2 balances and 2 weight transferences must be shown. Weight transference means moving your body weight from one body part to another, for example from your feet onto your hands in a cartwheel.

The short floor sequence (a routine of linked skills performed on the floor) includes at least 4 of the listed agilities, which are covered in the blocks on weight transference and other floor agilities.
Proficiency (skill and control) is shown in at least 2 vaults from handspring, short arm overswing or an optional vault of similar tariff. Tariff is the difficulty value given to a vault.
notes.tip: Know the minimums as numbers: 2 jumps, 2 rolls, 2 balances, 2 weight transferences, at least 4 listed agilities in the sequence and at least 2 vaults.

notes.b: A jump is a skill where you leave the floor, show a shape in the air and land under control. All the jumps share the same take-off and landing, and differ in the shape made in the air.
points: Every jump takes off from two feet with an arm swing, which helps lift the body into the air.
Tuck: the knees are pulled up to the chest while in the air.
Pike: the legs are kept straight and together, with the body folded forward at the hips, so the body makes an L or V shape.
Straddle: the legs are kept straight and apart in the air.
180-degree turn: the gymnast turns through 180 degrees (a half turn) in the air, so they land facing the opposite way.
Every jump ends in a controlled two-footed landing with the knees bent and the arms out. Bent knees absorb the force of landing and outstretched arms help balance.

notes.b: A roll turns the body over while it stays in contact with the mat, so it is the safest way to rotate. Both rolls use a tucked, rounded body so you roll over the back and not the neck.
points: Forward roll: the chin is tucked and the hands are placed flat on the mat.
Forward roll: the legs push, and the body rolls over the rounded back.
Forward roll: the gymnast comes up onto the feet without using the hands, which shows control.
Backward roll: the body is tucked tightly, with the hands by the ears and palms up, ready to push.
Backward roll: the gymnast rolls back, then pushes through the hands to land on the feet.

notes.b: A balance is a held, still position where the body is supported on a small base. The skill is in the control and the straight, tight body shape.
points: Handstand: the arms are straight and shoulder-width apart, with the body straight and the core (the trunk muscles) tight.
Handstand: the gymnast kicks up from a lunge (one leg forward with the knee bent, the other leg straight behind), holds the shoulders over the hands and stays still, then steps down.
Headstand: the base is a triangle formed by the forehead and both hands, which gives a stable support.
Headstand: the hips are held over the head and the legs are raised with control.
Arabesque: the gymnast balances on one straight leg, with the other leg extended behind, the arms out and the chest lifted.

notes.b: These skills move your weight from your feet onto your hands and back to your feet, travelling as you go. They are the weight transferences you choose from to meet the minimum of two.
points: Cartwheel: from a lunge (one leg forward with the knee bent), the hands are placed one after the other in a line.
Cartwheel: the legs pass straight over the top in the frontal plane (the flat plane that divides the body into front and back), and the gymnast lands one foot after the other, facing sideways.
Round-off: a cartwheel with a quarter turn, in which the legs snap together overhead and the gymnast lands on two feet facing back the way they came.
Round-off: it links into backward skills, because landing on two feet facing back gives a starting position for them.
Handspring: the gymnast runs and hurdles (a small step and hop into the skill), places the hands on the mat and swings the legs straight over.
Handspring: the gymnast pushes from the shoulders and lands on the feet with the arms up.
Back flip (back handspring): the gymnast sits back as if into a chair, swings the arms back and up, and jumps backwards onto the hands.
Back flip: the legs snap over to land on the feet.
notes.tip: Written answers can ask about planes and axes in gymnastics. The cartwheel is described as passing over in the frontal plane.

notes.b: The short floor sequence must include at least four agilities from the syllabus list. The handspring and back flip on that list are covered under weight transference, and these are the rest.
points: Backward roll to handstand: a backward roll that finishes in a handstand.
Front somersault: a forward rotation through the air without using the hands.
Handstand half turn: a 180-degree turn made while balanced on the hands.
One-handed cartwheel: a cartwheel performed with one hand on the floor.
Back somersault: a backward rotation through the air without using the hands.
Back and forward walkovers: an arch of the body with the hands on the floor and the legs passing over, moving backwards or forwards.

notes.b: A vault is a skill where the gymnast runs, uses a springboard to launch, and passes over a vault table (a padded apparatus) with the hands. You must show proficiency in at least two vaults from the syllabus list.
points: Handspring vault: the gymnast runs and takes off from two feet on the springboard.
Handspring vault: the hands are placed on the vault table with straight arms.
Handspring vault: the body rotates forward over the hands, the gymnast pushes off the table and lands facing away from it.
Short arm overswing: one of the vaults the specification names; learn its technique from your teacher's demonstration.
Optional vault: any vault of similar tariff, meaning similar difficulty value, excluding through and straddle vaults.
notes.tip: For the short arm overswing, name it as one of the listed vaults and do not describe its technique. Through and straddle vaults are excluded for the optional vault.

notes.b: A sequence is more than a list of skills. It is a planned routine in which the agilities are joined smoothly, and the way it is composed is part of what is judged.
points: The sequence has a planned start and finish, so it looks deliberate and not like a series of separate skills.
Smooth linking movements of steps, turns and jumps join the agilities together, so the routine flows.
Levels (low, middle and high) and directions are varied across the sequence to add interest.
The whole floor area is used, rather than staying in one place.
Speed is contrasted, with slow and fast sections.
Landings are controlled.
notes.tip: Written answers on gymnastics ask about compositional elements, so use these as your list: start and finish, links, levels, directions, floor area and speed.

notes.b: A routine is marked on three things: what you attempt, how well you perform it and how well it is put together. Knowing this tells you where marks are won and lost.
points: Difficulty: the elements attempted are scored for their difficulty, so harder skills are worth more.
Execution: deductions (marks taken off) are made for bent legs, flexed feet (feet not pointed), loss of balance and poor landings.
Artistry and composition: judged with aesthetic and artistic criteria such as body line, control and fluency (smooth flow).
notes.tip: Aesthetic criteria are taught in Aesthetic and artistic considerations, so apply them briefly here. Written answers ask about aesthetic criteria.

notes.b: Gymnastics involves inverted positions, rotation and landings from height, so injuries are a risk. These precautions reduce that risk.
points: Warm-up and conditioning (exercises that build strength and fitness) come before any skill is attempted.
Progressions come first: easier steps are learned before harder ones, for example a handstand is practised against a wall before a free handstand.
Mats are placed correctly for each skill.
Trained spotters (people who stand ready to help) support the gymnast at the hips and shoulders.
The springboard and vault are checked before use.
No jewellery is worn.

notes.b: Artistic gymnastics asks a lot of the body and the mind. These demands are the qualities a gymnast needs to perform the skills above.
points: Physical demands: flexibility, strength in the upper body and core, power and balance. Upper body strength is needed, for example, to support the body on the hands.
Co-ordination and spatial awareness: controlling body parts in relation to each other and to the space around the body.
Mental demands: courage, because many skills are inverted or rotate, and concentration.
notes.tip: Written answers can ask about flexibility in gymnastics, so link it to the skills that need it.

keyTerms.definition: A body position in a jump with the knees pulled up to the chest.
A body position in a jump with the legs kept straight and together and the body folded forward at the hips.
A body position in a jump with the legs kept straight and apart.
A sideways weight transference in which the hands are placed one after the other in a line and the legs pass over the top in the frontal plane.
A cartwheel with a quarter turn, in which the legs snap together overhead and the gymnast lands on two feet facing back the way they came.
A forward weight transference from a run and hurdle, with the hands placed on the floor, the legs swung over and the gymnast landing on the feet.
A backward weight transference, also called a back handspring, in which the gymnast jumps backwards onto the hands and snaps the legs over to land.
A continuous arch of the body over the hands, moving backwards or forwards, with the legs passing over.
A balance on one straight leg with the other leg extended behind and the arms out.
One of the vaults named by the specification for artistic gymnastics.
The difficulty value given to a vault.
Physically supporting a gymnast at the hips and shoulders during a skill to prevent a fall.

factCards.definition: At least 2 jumps, 2 rolls, 2 balances and 2 weight transferences; at least 4 listed agilities in the short floor sequence; at least 2 vaults from the list.
Handstand, headstand, arabesque or another balance; at least 2 are required.
Cartwheel, round-off, handspring and back flip; at least 2 are required.
Handspring, short arm overswing or an optional vault of similar tariff, excluding through and straddle vaults.

factCards.term: Floor agilities counted towards the four
factCards.definition: Backward roll to handstand, handspring, back flip, front somersault, handstand half turn, one-handed cartwheel, back somersault, and back and forward walkovers.

questions.prompt: Describe the key technique points of a cartwheel and identify the plane and axis in which it occurs.
questions.model: A cartwheel starts from a lunge, with the hands placed on the floor one after the other in a line. The gymnast rotates sideways, with the legs passing straight over the top of the body, and lands one foot after the other, facing sideways. The movement occurs in the frontal plane, which divides the body into front and back. The rotation takes place about the sagittal axis, which runs from front to back.

questions.prompt: Name two balances and two jumps used in gymnastics and give one technique point for each.
questions.model: Balances: the handstand, in which the shoulders stay over the hands with straight arms shoulder-width apart; and the arabesque, in which the free leg is extended straight behind with the chest lifted. Jumps: the tuck, in which the knees are pulled up to the chest; and the pike, in which the legs stay straight and together with the body folded forward at the hips.
